passage.text: Perusing the food choices in each aisle of the grocery store can be a daunting experience for shoppers. From peanut butter to yogurt, everything seems to come in myriad options, including fat-free, gluten-free, sugar-free, and organic. Many people are aware that organic food is grown without the use of pesticides, synthetic fertilizers, and other unnatural substances. What this means is that by buying organic foods, consumers are directly supporting a healthier society and environment, in addition to their own well-being. Foods labeled organic can cost ten to forty percent more than nonorganic foods, but understanding what organic food offers—and what it doesn't—is key to deciding that the benefits are worth the price.

Many grocery shoppers opt to pay more for organic fruits and vegetables because the label means the crops were grown without the use of pesticides. Pesticides, by design, contain toxins, since these protect crops from damaging elements such as rodents, insects, and invasive plant species. However, pesticides in their concentrated form have been tied to several chronic diseases in humans. For example, recent research has indicated a strong link between exposure to insecticides in humans and other brain disorders such as dementia, in addition to general cognitive problems.

Cancer is another disease tied to pesticides; what is especially disturbing is the rate at which young people in agricultural areas are suffering. Children who reside in farming communities have an elevated risk of developing cancers of the lymphatic system. These types of cancers have been among the most closely linked to pesticide use. Research shows that children are affected by pesticides in other serious ways, such as attention-deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD). A study conducted by scientists from the University of Montreal and Harvard University looked at the level of pesticide residue in the urine of 1,100 children, from ages eight to fifteen. It found that for every tenfold increase in pesticide residue, there was a thirty-five percent increase in the chances of the child developing ADHD. Upon release of the study, Maryse Bouchard, the lead researcher, recommended purchasing organic fruits and vegetables for children.

Like organic fruits and vegetables, organic meat is produced without pesticides as well as without antibiotics. Since the 1940s, antibiotics have been given to animals used for meat to prevent disease and promote growth. In fact, about eighty percent of all antibiotics sold in the United States today are used on farm animals. The problem with this widespread practice is that it is likely leading to the development of superbugs. These strains of illnesses develop in the animals because bacteria evolve and become resistant to antibiotics after long periods of exposure. While organic meats are not believed to be less likely to contain bacteria, the germs that organic meats do contain are more likely to be treatable. Clearly, the peace of mind makes the price of organic meat worth it.

If spending more on organic food simply for health's sake still seems dubious, consider the environmental factors. The use of chemical fertilizers in agricultural areas across the globe is causing problems due to fertilizers' toxic effects on water and soil. Fertilizer is rich in nitrogen and phosphorus, which have an unfortunate impact when they seep into bodies of water. The effect is called nitrogen pollution. For example, the Caribbean Sea is suffering from giant algae blooms that consume all of the oxygen in the water, killing other marine life. These blooms are tied to nitrogen pollution from fertilizer use on farms along the Amazon River, which empties into the Atlantic Ocean. In addition, groundwater in some parts of the world is tainted by the chemical fertilizers and pesticides used to grow nonorganic crops, rendering it unsafe to drink. Such fertilizers also contribute to eventual soil erosion. All of this means that buying organic foods can be seen as a contribution toward a healthier environment.

Some people look at the high prices of organic foods and believe that the organic label must be a racket. After all, the United States Department of Agriculture regulates all foods, so they must all be equally safe, whether they are labeled organic or not. Additionally, organic foods tend to have a shorter shelf life, so they are harder to store and may go to waste more frequently. Food shoppers have a significant choice to make. Should they make the switch to organic foods? Or should they continue to buy all conventional foods, thereby exposing themselves, their children, and the environment to significant dangers? Since people will go to the market after having decided to buy all organic foods or not, it is tremendously important that everybody is armed with the right information to make the costlier—but worthwhile—investment.

header.text: In a persuasive essay, an author tries to convince readers to do something or believe something.  A persuasive essay usually includes a main claim, supporting claims, and evidence.

contents.text: The main claim is the author's central argument.
The supporting claims are the reasons that support the author's main claim.
The evidence backs up the supporting claims. Evidence is often information like facts or statistics.

Besides these parts of the essay, an author may use other strategies to persuade readers. For example, the author may introduce an opposing claim, or a claim that disagrees with the essay's main claim. The author might explain the opposing claim and give reasons why the opposing claim is weak.

When you read a persuasive essay, consider how it uses supporting claims, evidence, and other strategies. Sometimes an author may use reasoning that is not valid or may include evidence that is not relevant to the main claim. Think critically about the reasoning in a persuasive essay. One strategy is to imagine how an opponent might attack or critique the essay's supporting claims and evidence. This will help you decide whether the author's argument is reliable and reasonable.

These strains of illnesses develop in the animals because bacteria evolve and become resistant to antibiotics after long periods of exposure. passage.text: A quiet space is often considered essential for achieving the concentration that leads to academic success. But research shows that some students may benefit from breaking the silence with certain kinds of music while they study. Music has a powerful influence on both the body and the brain, in ways that can help students navigate the physical and emotional obstacles that come with academic challenges. Still, students should choose their tunes wisely. Relaxing music with minimal variation and a steady, repetitive rhythm seems to make the best study partner.

Studies have identified a link between soothing background music and cognitive performance. One U.S. study compared students who took a test to a background of soft music with those who took the test under silent conditions. The study found that students taking a test to music not only completed more questions within a set time but also answered more questions correctly. Music has been further linked to improvements in memory and recall. French researchers concluded that when classical music was played during a traditional lecture, students were better able to remember the information presented. In a similar vein, American researchers found that music moves the brain to pay attention, engaging the parts of the brain that are associated with attention and memory. Experts agree that when music stimulates mood and motivation, students are able to learn more and to better demonstrate their knowledge.

A bit of mood music affects more than just memory and recall when students hit the books. Music can also relieve stress associated with school. Scientists have learned that music engages the autonomic nervous system, which not only controls the unconscious functions of the body but also influences emotions. So it's no surprise that researchers from the Group Health Research Institute concluded that certain kinds of background music can be just as effective at reducing stress as a massage. Music affects the brain by causing it to release dopamine, a chemical that promotes relaxation. If the pressure of studying for a major test is giving you the jitters, music can calm your nerves.

Furthermore, while the brain feels better with music, the body may as well. Research shows that certain types of music can make physical pain feel less intense, particularly for older adults and patients receiving medical treatment while in intensive care. Music can also be an asset to athletes, many of whom use music to help improve physical performance and endurance. A study of male college students and exercise revealed that participants worked harder while listening to music they enjoyed. What's more, calming music with a steady, meditative rhythm at day's end can help people sleep longer and more deeply. Studies have shown that listening to classical music at bedtime can be an effective treatment for people who have trouble falling asleep.

Some educators still express concern that listening to music while trying to concentrate may do more harm than good. For example, some studies have shown that students absorb less information when they listen to music with lyrics. Lyrics also seem to get in the way of completing writing assignments. Loud or agitated music may have a negative influence on a student's mood or act as a distraction. In addition, some experts speculate that students who are accustomed to studying with music will find it difficult to recall relevant information in a silent testing environment. The best approach may also depend on the students themselves. Students who are easily distracted may find any kind of background music to be a barrier.

Head-banging, adrenaline-soaked music is not an ideal choice for most students while buckling down for a chemistry assignment or settling in with an English essay. But research shows that rhythmic, soothing background music can enhance student performance in a variety of ways. In addition to boosting mental acuity, concentration, and recall, background music can help relieve the stress and anxiety associated with preparing for high-stakes tests. Listening to music during study time may not mean a guaranteed A for all students, but those who find it helpful should be allowed to plug in their headphones.

passage.text: A quiet space is often considered essential for achieving the concentration that leads to academic success. But research shows that some students may benefit from breaking the silence with certain kinds of music while they study. Music has a powerful influence on both the body and the brain, in ways that can help students navigate the physical and emotional obstacles that come with academic challenges. Still, students should choose their tunes wisely. Relaxing music with minimal variation and a steady, repetitive rhythm seems to make the best study partner.

Studies have identified a link between soothing background music and cognitive performance. One U.S. study compared students who took a test to a background of soft music with those who took the test under silent conditions. The study found that students taking a test to music not only completed more questions within a set time but also answered more questions correctly. Music has been further linked to improvements in memory and recall. French researchers concluded that when classical music was played during a traditional lecture, students were better able to remember the information presented. In a similar vein, American researchers found that music moves the brain to pay attention, engaging the parts of the brain that are associated with attention and memory. Experts agree that when music stimulates mood and motivation, students are able to learn more and to better demonstrate their knowledge.

A bit of mood music affects more than just memory and recall when students hit the books. Music can also relieve stress associated with school. Scientists have learned that music engages the autonomic nervous system, which not only controls the unconscious functions of the body but also influences emotions. So it's no surprise that researchers from the Group Health Research Institute concluded that certain kinds of background music can be just as effective at reducing stress as a massage. Music affects the brain by causing it to release dopamine, a chemical that promotes relaxation. If the pressure of studying for a major test is giving you the jitters, music can calm your nerves.

Furthermore, while the brain feels better with music, the body may as well. Research shows that certain types of music can make physical pain feel less intense, particularly for older adults and patients receiving medical treatment while in intensive care. Music can also be an asset to athletes, many of whom use music to help improve physical performance and endurance. A study of male college students and exercise revealed that participants worked harder while listening to music they enjoyed. What's more, calming music with a steady, meditative rhythm at day's end can help people sleep longer and more deeply. Studies have shown that listening to classical music at bedtime can be an effective treatment for people who have trouble falling asleep.

Some educators still express concern that listening to music while trying to concentrate may do more harm than good. For example, some studies have shown that students absorb less information when they listen to music with lyrics. Lyrics also seem to get in the way of completing writing assignments. Loud or agitated music may have a negative influence on a student's mood or act as a distraction. In addition, some experts speculate that students who are accustomed to studying with music will find it difficult to recall relevant information in a silent testing environment. The best approach may also depend on the students themselves. Students who are easily distracted may find any kind of background music to be a barrier.

Head-banging, adrenaline-soaked music is not an ideal choice for most students while buckling down for a chemistry assignment or settling in with an English essay. But research shows that rhythmic, soothing background music can enhance student performance in a variety of ways. In addition to boosting mental acuity, concentration, and recall, background music can help relieve the stress and anxiety associated with preparing for high-stakes tests. Listening to music during study time may not mean a guaranteed A for all students, but those who find it helpful should be allowed to plug in their headphones.

passage.text: Competitive youth football has been a beloved American pastime for decades. However, in recent years, there have been concerns about serious injuries, particularly brain trauma, at every level of football. These concerns have led some to believe that young people should not be permitted to participate in the sport. But when examining youth sports as a whole, football tends to draw unfair attention when it comes to injuries. In fact, other youth sports present a higher injury rate than football, and football is becoming considerably safer as regulations are updated and safety equipment is improved. To ban youth football, therefore, would be an extreme measure out of proportion to football's relative risks and inconsistent with the treatment of other youth sports.

It's easy to watch a popular, rough-and-tumble activity like tackle football and believe that it must result in the most damaging injuries of any youth sport. However, evidence indicates that other competitive youth activities inflict serious harm at a higher rate. According to the National Center for Catastrophic Sport Injury Research, youth football's rate of catastrophic injury is lower than that of either ice hockey or gymnastics. In fact, high school cheerleading, not football, carries the greatest risk of catastrophic injury. Cheerleaders make up only about three percent of female high school athletes, but cheerleading is responsible for sixty-five percent of these athletes' catastrophic injuries. Numbers from the United States Consumer Product Safety Commission show that, in one recent year, over twenty percent of the nearly twenty-six thousand cheerleading-related emergency room visits involved injuries to the head, neck, or face. This included 1,070 concussions and dozens of head and neck fractures. Nonetheless, despite their higher rate of serious injuries, few people are calling for bans on hockey, gymnastics, or cheerleading. It is the appearance of danger, not a higher injury rate, that has attracted negative attention toward youth football.

The fact is, there is no safe sport, contact or otherwise. Data from the National Center for Catastrophic Sport Injury Research show that the majority of catastrophic sports injuries for young people are indirect. On the football field, heat stroke or heart failure is more likely to cause a catastrophic injury than a hard tackle or a collision. These risks are not specific to youth football. They are common to other sports such as soccer, track and field, lacrosse, or any youth activity pursued for long periods of time outdoors. A ban on tackle football would do nothing to prevent these more common kinds of catastrophic injury.

The Center's data also indicate that catastrophic injuries in football have been trending dramatically downward since the 1960s. This change can be attributed to a number of measures short of full bans on tackling. For example, football helmets, once relatively simple plastic shells, have been continually improved with new kinds of padding and additional flexibility. In addition, many youth football programs now limit the type and duration of tackling drills during practices. Looking beyond football, there is a widely recognized need to protect youth from catastrophic head injuries in any sport, which is why all fifty states have passed legislation regulating how to handle concussions in youth activities. These necessary changes have reduced the severity of injuries. But in spite of an improved safety record over the years, the nation's biggest youth football program, Pop Warner, suffered a 9.5% drop in participation between 2010 and 2012. According to Pop Warner's medical director, fear surrounding brain trauma is the top reason for the plunge.

Motivated by this fear, some have suggested that tackling be banned from youth football altogether, at least until high school. However, in 2015, the American Academy of Pediatrics released a report that included differing recommendations aimed at improving youth football safety. The report emphasized the importance of enforcing proper tackle form. Most football injuries occur in the ankles, knees, hands, and back, but head and neck injuries are usually the most serious, and most often they are the result of illegal tackling. The report speculates that if the practice of tackling were delayed until high school, football players would not learn the safest techniques at a young age.

Those who seek a ban on youth football because of its health risks are ignoring the substantial benefits of the sport. The physical exercise provided by strength training and conditioning for football is excellent for the cardiovascular system. Football's complexity and quick plays improve the concentration, mental discipline, and time management skills of its young players.

Proponents of a ban also ignore that football remains popular among viewers. While youth participation in tackle football may have dropped, interest in professional football remains substantial, with NFL games averaging tens of millions of viewers and achieving TV ratings higher than any other live sport. Although viewership has dipped recently, a 2014 study showed that the trend over the past thirty years has been a steady rise, while the ratings of other professional sports either declined or remained the same. These numbers signal football's continued importance today.

Given that young people are prone to risk-taking, playing tackle football with the appropriate safety measures is an excellent positive outlet for aggressive energy. With each snap of the football, players must instantly assess rapidly shifting situations and make quick decisions while gauging their own and their opponents' capabilities. Although the risk of serious injuries can never be eliminated, it can be reduced through education and consistent enforcement of the rules by coaches and trained officials. Applying a ban to full-tackle youth football would be inconsistent with the way risks of injury are treated in other youth sports. It would be an extreme and unnecessary reaction against a pastime whose benefits outweigh its risks and which appeals to people of all ages.

For example, football helmets, once relatively simple plastic shells, have been continually improved with new kinds of padding and additional flexibility. In addition, many youth football programs now limit the type and duration of tackling drills during practices. Looking beyond football, there is a widely recognized need to protect youth from catastrophic head injuries in any sport, which is why all fifty states have passed legislation regulating how to handle concussions in youth activities. These necessary changes have reduced the severity of injuries. But in spite of an improved safety record over the years, the nation's biggest youth football program, Pop Warner, suffered a 9.5% drop in participation between 2010 and 2012. According to Pop Warner's medical director, fear surrounding brain trauma is the top reason for the plunge.

Motivated by this fear, some have suggested that tackling be banned from youth football altogether, at least until high school. However, in 2015, the American Academy of Pediatrics released a report that included differing recommendations aimed at improving youth football safety. The report emphasized the importance of enforcing proper tackle form. Most football injuries occur in the ankles, knees, hands, and back, but head and neck injuries are usually the most serious, and most often they are the result of illegal tackling. The report speculates that if the practice of tackling were delayed until high school, football players would not learn the safest techniques at a young age.

Those who seek a ban on youth football because of its health risks are ignoring the substantial benefits of the sport. The physical exercise provided by strength training and conditioning for football is excellent for the cardiovascular system. Football's complexity and quick plays improve the concentration, mental discipline, and time management skills of its young players.

Proponents of a ban also ignore that football remains popular among viewers. While youth participation in tackle football may have dropped, interest in professional football remains substantial, with NFL games averaging tens of millions of viewers and achieving TV ratings higher than any other live sport. Although viewership has dipped recently, a 2014 study showed that the trend over the past thirty years has been a steady rise, while the ratings of other professional sports either declined or remained the same. These numbers signal football's continued importance today.

Given that young people are prone to risk-taking, playing tackle football with the appropriate safety measures is an excellent positive outlet for aggressive energy. With each snap of the football, players must instantly assess rapidly shifting situations and make quick decisions while gauging their own and their opponents' capabilities. Although the risk of serious injuries can never be eliminated, it can be reduced through education and consistent enforcement of the rules by coaches and trained officials. Applying a ban to full-tackle youth football would be inconsistent with the way risks of injury are treated in other youth sports. It would be an extreme and unnecessary reaction against a pastime whose benefits outweigh its risks and which appeals to people of all ages.

passage.text: American college campuses are full of energy and enthusiasm, and many institutions maintain a widely celebrated tradition aside from learning. The mania for sports programs at some universities would appear to be as important and time-honored as the academics—or more so, considering the vast amounts of money that a single sport can generate for a school. The average Division I school earns nearly thirty million dollars in revenue each year, with some schools generating closer to one hundred million. Yet the rules dictated by the National Collegiate Athletic Association forbid the players from receiving any money for their participation. And if the NCAA wishes to keep the avid support of its most beloved programs, as well as maintain fairness and integrity in college sports, it must keep this fiscal policy in place.

The numbers are staggering, and it is easy to look at the profits generated by the country's biggest sports programs and think it unfair that none of the money is paid to the players. After all, aren't they the ones drawing the enormous audience, the excitement, and thus, the money? And the audience is indeed large—most of the revenue generated by the NCAA is through sales to TV networks to air games and tournaments. In fact, the NCAA is in the middle of an eleven-billion-dollar contract with CBS/Turner Sports, who own the rights to air the March Madness championship tournament from 2011-2024. ESPN pays the NCAA $470 million each year to air the College Football Playoffs. And who is everybody tuning in to watch? The players.

But while the NCAA is not paying out any of its revenue to the players, many of the players on these money-making college teams are benefiting financially. That boon comes in the form of an athletic scholarship awarded by the university. An athletic scholarship is any given amount of financial assistance provided to the student athlete in exchange for playing. The amount of scholarship money awarded is largely based on the player's talent, and it can be substantial, covering tuition, room and board, and more. In fact, a full athletic scholarship at a high-tuition Division I school amounts to about sixty-five thousand dollars per year. According to some mathematical models, even if the student athlete were given an annual salary of one hundred thousand dollars in lieu of a scholarship, that money would amount to no profit at all, or even a loss, given the exorbitant costs of higher education.

The idea of paying student athletes to play also raises issues of fairness. Basketball and football are usually the only sports that make the school and the NCAA money. Most of the other sports programs at a university are operating on tight budgets. Does that mean only the students on the University of Texas's football team get paid, while a talented athlete on that school's Division I swimming team doesn't? Without the incentive of money, coupled with the envy of paid athletes in lucrative programs, swimmers are bound to lose their competitive desire. Paying student athletes would backfire on academic institutions because, without a salary, the competitors on teams that don't make money would stop trying their hardest to win. It's unlikely that any student athletes would even want to participate any longer, if they are not among the lucky few who get paid.

The responsibility of payment would fall into the lap of either the NCAA or the colleges themselves. While the most profitable college programs net large amounts of money, they also must spend a great deal to operate. The 2015–2016 Ohio State University athletic program generated around $171 million in revenue, but it also spent around $167 million in operating costs. These costs include training facilities, stadium upkeep, and salaries for the coaching staff, many of whom sign large-salary contracts themselves. And the NCAA cannot issue salaries to student athletes because it operates as a nonprofit, meaning that it gives back the vast majority of what it takes in. Ninety-six percent of the money the NCAA generates is either returned to schools and their conferences or used for other programs that help athletes at the college level.

Despite the widespread enthusiasm for college sports, young athletes are still at college to receive an education, and that education must include principles of honor and good faith. The NCAA set its strict rules about money for good reason: to enforce fairness and consistency of conduct in all sports, programs, and players. Without integrity surrounding competition, integrity within competition is threatened. That means paying college athletes could invite forces, such as dishonest or fraudulent players and practices, that would violate the purity of the game.

header.text: In a persuasive essay, an author tries to convince readers to do something or believe something.  A persuasive essay usually includes a main claim, supporting claims, and evidence.

contents.text: The main claim is the author's central argument.
The supporting claims are the reasons that support the author's main claim.
The evidence backs up the supporting claims. Evidence is often information like facts or statistics.

Besides these parts of the essay, an author may use other strategies to persuade readers. For example, the author may introduce an opposing claim, or a claim that disagrees with the essay's main claim. The author might explain the opposing claim and give reasons why the opposing claim is weak.

When you read a persuasive essay, consider how it uses supporting claims, evidence, and other strategies. Sometimes an author may use reasoning that is not valid or may include evidence that is not relevant to the main claim. Think critically about the reasoning in a persuasive essay. One strategy is to imagine how an opponent might attack or critique the essay's supporting claims and evidence. This will help you decide whether the author's argument is reliable and reasonable.

header.text: <instructions>Read the text.</instructions>

passage.text: In the relatively new era of human space exploration, astonishing feats seem to come one after another. From the 1950s until the 1970s, the United States and the Soviet Union sought to best one another in travel and research exploits beyond the Earth's atmosphere, from orbiting the planet to walking on the moon. Today, over five hundred people from roughly forty countries have orbited Earth. The International Space Station, the most elaborate global scientific project in history, is the result of the engineering prowess of five different nations. Experts, from astronauts to physicists, are now working toward the next interstellar triumph: sending humans to Mars. There are important motivations for this daunting yet essential task: scientific progress and the long-term survival of the human species.

Today, there are more people than ever on Earth, using its resources and degrading the water, soil, and air. Medical advancements have allowed people to live longer. The time is approaching when Earth may no longer be able to support our numbers.

A human voyage from Earth to Mars, once improbable, has become feasible through both government and private undertakings. The privately funded company SpaceX, which designs, manufactures, and launches spacecraft, has devised a workable rocket design that is three-and-a-half times more powerful than NASA's biggest rocket ship. The SpaceX rocket would be reusable and large enough to carry one to two hundred astronauts, and it would deploy solar panels to fuel the long trip. Elon Musk, the founder of SpaceX, believes his company may begin sending human settlers to Mars sometime in the 2020s. In 2016, President Barack Obama endorsed a NASA Mars mission with the goal of sending humans to the planet and back by the 2030s. In fact, NASA recently selected six companies to design human habitats for the months-long trip.

Whether humans land on Mars in a government rocket ship or a privately funded one, they will be tasked with more than simply escaping an overpopulated Earth. In fact, the astronauts could make discoveries on Mars that enrich life on their home planet. Advancements in arenas such as technology, medicine, and agriculture—all essential spheres for human survival and progress—may result from research conducted on Mars.

Key findings can even happen inadvertently in novel surroundings. For example, when the Hubble Space Telescope was first launched, the pictures it transmitted to Earth were blurry due to a glitch in its engineering. The problem was eventually fixed, but in the meantime, an algorithm was developed to help analyze the information in the blurred space photographs. The same algorithm was later used to detect early stages of breast cancer in X-ray images. If an engineering flaw in a giant telescope saved lives in a most unlikely way, the advancements of a Mars mission are sure to be innumerable. After all, a large, untested rocket ship will be equipped with instruments certain to have unforeseen glitches, leading to discoveries in quite possibly all of the sciences.

Sending humans to Mars offers the opportunity to explore the unknown, much like the travel and research conducted in the deep sea. Materials from deep-sea marine organisms are currently being used or developed to battle inflammation, fungal infections, tuberculosis, HIV, and cancer. There is reason to believe Mars is also home to matter with the potential to help humans. Photographic evidence from NASA's Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter shows the possible presence of ancient deep-sea thermal vents, just like the ones on Earth, where some scientists believe life on our planet originated. Researchers have examined photos and determined that the area contains a mix of minerals that could serve as a source of energy for life forms. If microbial life exists on Mars, it could assist with medical advancements like Earth's deep-sea organisms. But any advancements Mars has to offer will not be realized until humans arrive and explore.

In theory, a successful humans-to-Mars mission could result in scientific breakthroughs like curing a disease or discovering extraterrestrial life. The prospect of humans settling on a new planet could allay fears surrounding Earth's overpopulation and the fate of humanity. One thing is certain: a successful mission would have a global impact.

passage.text: In the relatively new era of human space exploration, astonishing feats seem to come one after another. From the 1950s until the 1970s, the United States and the Soviet Union sought to best one another in travel and research exploits beyond the Earth's atmosphere, from orbiting the planet to walking on the moon. Today, over five hundred people from roughly forty countries have orbited Earth. The International Space Station, the most elaborate global scientific project in history, is the result of the engineering prowess of five different nations. Experts, from astronauts to physicists, are now working toward the next interstellar triumph: sending humans to Mars. There are important motivations for this daunting yet essential task: scientific progress and the long-term survival of the human species.

Today, there are more people than ever on Earth, using its resources and degrading the water, soil, and air. Medical advancements have allowed people to live longer. The time is approaching when Earth may no longer be able to support our numbers.

A human voyage from Earth to Mars, once improbable, has become feasible through both government and private undertakings. The privately funded company SpaceX, which designs, manufactures, and launches spacecraft, has devised a workable rocket design that is three-and-a-half times more powerful than NASA's biggest rocket ship. The SpaceX rocket would be reusable and large enough to carry one to two hundred astronauts, and it would deploy solar panels to fuel the long trip. Elon Musk, the founder of SpaceX, believes his company may begin sending human settlers to Mars sometime in the 2020s. In 2016, President Barack Obama endorsed a NASA Mars mission with the goal of sending humans to the planet and back by the 2030s. In fact, NASA recently selected six companies to design human habitats for the months-long trip.

Whether humans land on Mars in a government rocket ship or a privately funded one, they will be tasked with more than simply escaping an overpopulated Earth. In fact, the astronauts could make discoveries on Mars that enrich life on their home planet. Advancements in arenas such as technology, medicine, and agriculture—all essential spheres for human survival and progress—may result from research conducted on Mars.

Key findings can even happen inadvertently in novel surroundings. For example, when the Hubble Space Telescope was first launched, the pictures it transmitted to Earth were blurry due to a glitch in its engineering. The problem was eventually fixed, but in the meantime, an algorithm was developed to help analyze the information in the blurred space photographs. The same algorithm was later used to detect early stages of breast cancer in X-ray images. If an engineering flaw in a giant telescope saved lives in a most unlikely way, the advancements of a Mars mission are sure to be innumerable. After all, a large, untested rocket ship will be equipped with instruments certain to have unforeseen glitches, leading to discoveries in quite possibly all of the sciences.

Sending humans to Mars offers the opportunity to explore the unknown, much like the travel and research conducted in the deep sea. Materials from deep-sea marine organisms are currently being used or developed to battle inflammation, fungal infections, tuberculosis, HIV, and cancer. There is reason to believe Mars is also home to matter with the potential to help humans. Photographic evidence from NASA's Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter shows the possible presence of ancient deep-sea thermal vents, just like the ones on Earth, where some scientists believe life on our planet originated. Researchers have examined photos and determined that the area contains a mix of minerals that could serve as a source of energy for life forms. If microbial life exists on Mars, it could assist with medical advancements like Earth's deep-sea organisms. But any advancements Mars has to offer will not be realized until humans arrive and explore.

In theory, a successful humans-to-Mars mission could result in scientific breakthroughs like curing a disease or discovering extraterrestrial life. The prospect of humans settling on a new planet could allay fears surrounding Earth's overpopulation and the fate of humanity. One thing is certain: a successful mission would have a global impact.

header.text: In a persuasive essay, an author tries to convince readers to do something or believe something.  A persuasive essay usually includes a main claim, supporting claims, and evidence.

contents.text: The main claim is the author's central argument.
The supporting claims are the reasons that support the author's main claim.
The evidence backs up the supporting claims. Evidence is often information like facts or statistics.

Besides these parts of the essay, an author may use other strategies to persuade readers. For example, the author may introduce an opposing claim, or a claim that disagrees with the essay's main claim. The author might explain the opposing claim and give reasons why the opposing claim is weak.

When you read a persuasive essay, consider how it uses supporting claims, evidence, and other strategies. Sometimes an author may use reasoning that is not valid or may include evidence that is not relevant to the main claim. Think critically about the reasoning in a persuasive essay. One strategy is to imagine how an opponent might attack or critique the essay's supporting claims and evidence. This will help you decide whether the author's argument is reliable and reasonable.

contents.text: Words change in meaning when speakers begin using them in new ways. For example, the word peruse once only meant to examine in detail, but it's now also commonly used to mean to look through in a casual manner.

header.text: When a word changes in meaning, its correct usage is often debated. Although a newer sense of the word may be more commonly used, many people consider a word's traditional definition to be the correct usage. Being able to distinguish the different uses of a word can help you use it appropriately for different audiences.
